lesson.title: FDR's Gamble: The Court-Packing Plan of 1937
lesson.summary: After the Supreme Court struck down several New Deal laws, a newly reelected Roosevelt proposed adding justices to the Court in 1937, a plan that failed badly and remains one of his most controversial moves.
lesson.body:
The Supreme Court's power to strike down acts of Congress as unconstitutional, first established in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, had become a serious obstacle to the New Deal by the mid 1930s. In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935) the Court unanimously struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act, and in United States v. Butler (1936) it struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act, both on the grounds that they exceeded the federal government's constitutional powers.

Roosevelt won reelection in November 1936 by an overwhelming margin, carrying every state except Maine and Vermont, and he read the result as a mandate to press ahead with the New Deal. Several sitting justices were in their seventies or older, and Roosevelt worried the Court would keep striking down his legislation. On February 5, 1937, he proposed the Judicial Procedures Reform Bill: for every sitting justice who reached age 70 and did not retire, the president could appoint an additional justice, up to a maximum of 15 justices total.

Roosevelt publicly framed the bill as relief for an overworked, aging Court, but almost no one believed that was the real purpose. Critics across the political spectrum, including many Democrats who had otherwise supported the New Deal, saw it as a bid to pack the Court with friendly votes and undermine the separation of powers. Chief Justice Charles Evans Hughes personally rebutted the workload argument in a letter to Congress, and the Senate Judiciary Committee ultimately rejected the plan.

In the middle of the fight, Justice Owen Roberts began voting with the Court's more liberal members to uphold New Deal style legislation, including a state minimum wage law in West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish, decided in 1937. Some commentators called this shift the switch in time that saved nine, though most historians now believe Roberts's vote had actually been decided before Roosevelt announced his plan, making the timing coincidental rather than a direct response to political pressure.

The court packing plan died in Congress by the summer of 1937, a rare and stinging political defeat for Roosevelt despite his popularity. In the years that followed, however, several justices retired or died, and Roosevelt eventually appointed eight new justices through ordinary vacancies, reshaping the Court's direction without ever changing its size.
